chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Taxonomy of Alternative Data

lessons.title: Web and App Data: Scraping, App Analytics, and Search Trends

body.text: Every tap, search, and page view is a small, unintended vote on demand. Web and app data is the business of counting those votes before the company has to report the total.

children.text: Web and app data is usually the first category a new quant researcher touches, because the tools are cheap or free, the concepts are intuitive, and Indian consumer internet companies generate an enormous amount of it. This lesson covers the three sub-categories you will use most, how the underlying numbers are actually estimated, and the legal terrain around scraping that you need to understand before you build anything on top of it.
Three Sub-Categories of Web and App Data

body.caption: App metrics, web traffic, and search trends measure different points in the customer journey

cells: Category rank, estimated downloads, and estimated active users for a mobile app
Tracking Zomato and Swiggy's relative app store ranks and estimated download trends as an early read on food-delivery order growth
Estimated visits, session duration, and traffic source mix for a website
Watching estimated traffic to an e-commerce or travel booking site as a proxy for browsing intent ahead of a booking season
Relative search interest for a term or phrase over time, indexed rather than an absolute count
Watching search interest for 'buy gold online' or 'gold rate today' rise ahead of Dhanteras and Akshaya Tritiya

children.text: How App Download Numbers Are Actually Estimated

markDefs.definition: Neither the Google Play Store nor the Apple App Store publishes exact download or active user counts for third-party apps. Analytics vendors instead estimate these figures from a mix of panel data, category rank movements, and modelling.

children.text: This is the single most important thing to understand before using any app data vendor's numbers: they are

. Vendors infer download and usage figures from category rank movements, opted-in device panels, and statistical modelling calibrated against whatever real numbers they can get. This is not a flaw specific to one provider, it is a structural feature of app analytics everywhere.

body.title: Why Android estimates are usually more reliable than iOS estimates in India

children.text: The overwhelming majority of Indian smartphone users are on Android, which gives estimation vendors a far larger panel and more rank-movement data to calibrate against than they have for iOS. In practice this means an app's Android estimates in India tend to carry a tighter error band than its iOS estimates. If you are building a signal on an India-focused consumer app, weight the Android read more heavily and treat the iOS number as a smaller, noisier supplement rather than an equal partner.

body.label: The estimation gap
body.value: Rank and panel based, not exact counts
body.context: No app data vendor, however good, is reading a true download counter. Every number in this category is a modelled estimate, which is why signal-to-noise from the Chapter 1 framework deserves a lower score here than for a direct government filing.

children.text: Search Trends as an Early Demand Signal: The Gold Festival Case

Search trend tools such as Google Trends report a relative search interest index, typically scaled from 0 to 100 for a chosen term and time window, rather than an absolute search count. Indian gold demand has a well documented festival seasonality: buying activity rises sharply around Akshaya Tritiya and Dhanteras. Search interest for terms like 'buy gold online' and 'gold rate today' tends to rise ahead of these dates as households research prices and options before purchasing, which makes it a plausible early, if noisy, read on the mood heading into the season for jewellery retailers such as Titan's Tanishq or Kalyan Jewellers.

body.title: Stylized search interest for 'buy gold online' across a year

children.text: The stylized curve above shows the shape you would expect: a spike around April, near Akshaya Tritiya, and the largest spike around October to November, near Dhanteras and Diwali. This is an illustration of the pattern, not measured data, and a real backtest would need several years of the actual index alongside verified festival dates, since the Hindu calendar shifts these festivals to different Gregorian dates each year.

body.code:
from pytrends.request import TrendReq
import pandas as pd

# pytrends is an unofficial, community-maintained wrapper around
# Google Trends. Treat rate limits and terms of service seriously,
# this is for research exploration, not a production data pipeline.
pytrends = TrendReq(hl='en-IN', tz=330)

keywords = ['buy gold online', 'gold rate today']
pytrends.build_payload(keywords, timeframe='today 12-m', geo='IN')

interest_over_time = pytrends.interest_over_time()
print(interest_over_time.tail())

# Next step: align this index against known festival dates
# (Akshaya Tritiya, Dhanteras) for the same year before treating
# any spike as a genuine seasonal signal rather than noise.
body.caption: A starting point for pulling India-specific Google Trends data with pytrends. Always check Google's terms of service and rate limits before scheduling this as a recurring job.

body.title: Reading the Search Trend Chart
body.question: Looking at the stylized chart above, why does the October to November spike matter more to a researcher than the April spike, even though both line up with real gold-buying festivals?
options: It doesn't matter more, both spikes are equally informative by construction
The October to November spike is larger and closer to Dhanteras and Diwali, both major gold-buying occasions, so it likely carries a stronger and more concentrated demand signal
October to November is simply a random calendar effect with no retail relevance
Search interest in April should always be ignored
body.explanation: The relative height of a spike matters because search interest is an index, not an absolute count. A larger, sharper spike close to a major buying occasion like Dhanteras is more likely to reflect concentrated purchase intent than a smaller, broader rise. This is exactly the kind of read a researcher has to make by eye and then verify statistically before trusting it.

children.text: The Legal Terrain: Scraping, robots.txt, and India's Data Protection Law

markDefs.definition: A voluntary text file websites publish to tell automated crawlers which pages they prefer not to be accessed. It is a widely respected convention, but by itself it is not a binding law, so ignoring it is a technical and reputational risk more than an automatic legal violation.

children.text: Scraping sits in genuinely unsettled legal territory, everywhere, not just in India. A website's

file and its Terms of Service can still create civil liability for breach of contract even where no specific scraping law is violated. A widely cited example is the years-long US legal battle between hiQ Labs and LinkedIn over scraping publicly visible LinkedIn profile data, which went through multiple rounds of appeal and showed just how unresolved the question of 'is publicly visible data fair game to scrape' remains even in a mature legal system. In India, unauthorized access to a computer system or data can trigger liability under Section 43 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on top of any contractual breach from violating a site's Terms of Service.

body.caption: Risk changes sharply depending on what you scrape, not just where you scrape it from

cells: Product prices, stock availability, or star ratings on an e-commerce category page
Lower, but still subject to the site's Terms of Service and rate limiting expectations
Category rank movements, estimated traffic totals for a domain
Lower to moderate, depends heavily on the specific platform's terms and API alternatives
Data that identifies a natural person
Individual user profiles, names linked to contact details, or personal reviews tied to identifiable accounts
Higher, and squarely within scope of India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, regardless of whether the data was publicly viewable

body.title: Why 'it was public' does not end the analysis under India's DPDP Act

children.text: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, governs the processing of digital personal data, meaning data that can identify a natural person. The Act's obligations attach to processing such data, not merely to how it was originally obtained, so the fact that a profile or contact detail was visible on a public webpage does not automatically place scraping and reusing it outside the Act's scope. This is a meaningfully different question from scraping aggregate, non-personal data like prices or category ranks, which is why the table above treats the two cases as different risk tiers rather than one blanket 'scraping is fine because it's public' rule.

body.title: Two Scraping Requests, One Compliance Answer
body.scenario: Your desk's junior analyst proposes two scraping projects for the same e-commerce site: Project A scrapes daily prices and stock availability across the top 500 product listings in the electronics category. Project B scrapes the names, city locations, and review histories of the 10,000 most active reviewer accounts on the platform.
body.prompt: Which project needs a materially higher level of legal and compliance review before it starts, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Project B needs a much higher level of review. It targets data that identifies natural persons, reviewer names tied to city location and review history, which falls within the scope of India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, regardless of whether the profiles were publicly visible on the site. Project A scrapes aggregate, non-personal product data, prices and stock levels, which carries lower privacy risk, though it still needs to respect the site's robots.txt and Terms of Service and stay within reasonable rate limits to avoid a breach of contract claim or an unauthorized access argument under the IT Act. The two projects should not be treated as one 'scraping policy' decision, since the underlying legal exposure is different in kind, not just in degree.

body.text: Before scraping anything, ask one question first: does this data identify a specific person? If yes, the analysis is a privacy and compliance question before it is a data engineering question. If no, it is mainly a Terms of Service and rate-limiting question. Keep the two separate, because they carry very different levels of risk.

This lesson explains general concepts for education and is not legal advice. Consult your organisation's legal and compliance team before scraping any website, app store, or search platform, and before relying on any specific vendor's app or web analytics.

points: Web and app data splits into three sub-categories: app store metrics, website traffic analytics, and search trend data, each capturing a different point in the customer journey
App download and active user figures are always vendor estimates built from panels and rank movements, never exact counts from Google Play or the Apple App Store
Android estimates are typically more reliable than iOS estimates for India-focused apps, given Android's dominant share of Indian smartphone users

Search trend tools report a relative index, not an absolute count, and Indian festival seasonality around gold buying (Akshaya Tritiya, Dhanteras) is a good example of a pattern worth testing rigorously rather than assuming
robots.txt and a site's Terms of Service are not the same as binding law, but violating them can still create civil liability, as the long-running hiQ Labs vs LinkedIn dispute illustrates

Scraping data that identifies a natural person triggers India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, even if that data was publicly visible, which is a materially higher risk tier than scraping aggregate, non-personal data like prices or ranks
